questions.q: What distinguishes a system of record from a system of engagement?
options: A system of record is always Salesforce; a system of engagement is always the ERP
A system of record is the authoritative source for a piece of data; a system of engagement is where users interact with it day to day, and the two may differ
There is no meaningful difference between the two terms
A system of engagement always has more data fields than a system of record
questions.explain: The system of record is authoritative for a given data domain; the system of engagement is where day-to-day interaction happens. They are frequently different systems for the same data.

questions.q: Why is it a mistake to look for a single system of record for an entire enterprise?
options: Different data domains (financial, HR, customer, product) are typically mastered by different systems, each authoritative for its own domain
Because every enterprise should have zero systems of record
Because Salesforce is always authoritative for every domain by default
Because systems of record only apply to companies with a single department
questions.explain: A mature enterprise typically has several systems of record, each correct for its own data domain -- an ERP for financial transactions, an HRIS for employee data, a CRM for customer engagement history, and so on.

questions.q: A sales rep views an invoice balance inside Salesforce. In a typical enterprise architecture, what is that number most likely to be?
options: The authoritative figure, since Salesforce is the system of record for all financial data
A randomly generated placeholder value
A synced copy from the ERP's general ledger, which remains the system of record for billing data
Data that Salesforce itself calculates independently of any other system
questions.explain: Billing and invoicing data typically lives in an ERP's general ledger; Salesforce commonly displays a synced copy for sales visibility rather than acting as the system of record for that domain.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a systems-of-record map as an architecture deliverable?
options: To visually diagram Salesforce's page layouts
To replace the need for a data owner on any object
To list every custom field in the org
To document which system is authoritative for each data domain and which direction data should flow, so integrations aren't built on unstated assumptions
questions.explain: A systems-of-record map makes explicit, for each data domain, which system is authoritative and which systems are read-only consumers -- preventing integrations from being built on silent, contested assumptions.

questions.q: What specific failure does a missing systems-of-record map tend to produce?
options: An integration syncing a 'corrected' value from a system of engagement back into the true system of record, corrupting a controlled dataset
Faster report performance across all systems
Automatic resolution of all duplicate records
Elimination of the need for any data stewards
questions.explain: Without an explicit map, integrations can be built in the wrong direction -- pushing a well-intentioned correction from the engagement layer back into the actual system of record -- corrupting data that was supposed to stay controlled.
